question: Break the noncovalent bonds holding a folded chain together and you have _____, which leaves the chain whole but takes away the shape it works in.
questions: Heat, molar urea and hydrostatic pressure all produce _____, but put on one thermodynamic footing they turn out not to do it the same way.
A drug bound to its target shifts that protein's melting temperature, so heating a whole proteome and watching for _____ reveals what the drug binds.
abstract:
Denaturation is the disruption of a protein's three-dimensional structure by treatments that break the noncovalent bonds holding it together. What is left is a flexible polypeptide chain that has lost its natural shape while remaining one continuous chain. Take the denaturing agent away and the protein often refolds, or renatures, spontaneously into its original conformation, which is how the shape was shown to be specified by the sequence. Several quite different treatments will do it, among them heating, hydrostatic pressure, and molar concentrations of a chaotrope such as urea, which disrupts noncovalent interactions directly. They are not interchangeable, and when the three are put on a single thermodynamic footing heat-induced unfolding turns out to be the most cooperative of the three, a result obtained on apolipoprotein A-1 and lysozyme.

Unfolding need not be a single step from folded to not, and mass spectrometry, which captures the states actually populated rather than an average over them, finds intermediates appearing as the urea concentration rises. Optical methods report an ensemble average and can struggle to resolve those intermediates at all, so how simple the process looks depends partly on the instrument watching it. The sensitivity of a fold to its conditions has been turned into an instrument in its own right, since a small molecule bound to a protein shifts that protein's melting temperature, stabilising or destabilising it. Heating cells across a range of temperatures and measuring which proteins are still soluble therefore identifies what a drug binds, unbiased and across a whole proteome at once. Both of the classic accounts are careful to say that a denatured protein often refolds rather than that it always does.
